claim: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 received the President's assent on 8 September 2016; its long title is 'An Act further to amend the Constitution of India'. Section 1(2): it comes into force on a date the Central Government notifies, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 246A (new, s.2): 'Notwithstanding anything contained in articles 246 and 254', Parliament and, subject to clause (2), every State Legislature have power to make laws on GST imposed by the Union or by the State.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 246A(2): Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on GST where the supply of goods or services or both takes place in the course of inter-State trade or commerce.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 269A (new, s.9): GST on supplies in the course of inter-State trade or commerce is levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between the Union and the States as Parliament provides by law on the Council's recommendations; import is deemed inter-State supply; amounts apportioned to a State do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India (269A(2)).
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(1)-(2): the President to constitute the GST Council within 60 days of commencement; members are the Union Finance Minister (Chairperson), the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance, and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation or another Minister nominated by each State Government.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(4): the Council recommends to the Union and the States on (a) taxes, cesses and surcharges to be subsumed; (b) goods and services to be subjected to or exempted from GST; (c) model laws, principles of levy and apportionment, place of supply; (d) threshold limit; (e) rates including floor rates with bands; (f) special rate for a specified period for a natural calamity or disaster; (g) special provision for Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; (h) any other matter.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: Useful for 'federalism': clause (g) names 11 States for special provision.

claim: Article 279A(5): the Council shall recommend the date on which GST is levied on petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel. Seventh Schedule entry 84 (Union List) is substituted so that Union excise remains only on those five goods and on tobacco and tobacco products.
value: five petroleum goods outside GST until date recommended
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: Whether those five goods are in GST today is not established here. Current status of these five goods not checked after 2019; see NOTES.

claim: Article 366(12A) (new, s.14): 'goods and services tax' means any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Article 366(26A): 'Services' means anything other than goods; 366(26B): 'State' for Arts 246A, 268, 269, 269A and 279A includes a Union territory with Legislature.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(6): in discharging its functions the Council 'shall be guided by the need for a harmonised structure of goods and services tax and for the development of a harmonised national market for goods and services'.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Article 279A(9): every Council decision is taken by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting; the Central Government's vote weighs one-third of the total votes cast and all State Governments together two-thirds. Article 279A(7): one-half of the members form the quorum.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: GST Council, Rules for conduct of business
note: Derived: the Centre alone can block (its 1/3 is more than the 1/4 that may dissent); States together can block only if they withhold more than 1/4 of total weight, i.e. States cannot pass anything against the Centre. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Page fixed: quorum (7) is on Gazette p.3, weighted-vote rule (9) on p.4. Derived Centre-veto reading checked against Council Rules rule 15(3) example (2023-GS2-15-03): holds.

claim: Article 279A(11): the Council 'shall establish a mechanism to adjudicate' any dispute between the Government of India and States, between the Union and States on one side and other States, or between States, arising out of its recommendations or their implementation.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: Whether the mechanism has ever been established: see 2020-GS3-12 ledger (42nd Council minutes show it was only argued about).

claim: Article 286 amended (s.13): references to 'sale or purchase of goods' become 'supply of goods or of services or both' (clauses 1 and 2), and clause (3) (central-sales-tax declared-goods restriction) is omitted. Article 268A (service tax) is omitted (s.7) and the words on excise on medicinal and toilet preparations are omitted from Art 268(1) (s.6).
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Seventh Schedule (s.17): Union List entries 92 (newspapers/advertisements tax) and 92C (service tax) omitted; State List entry 52 (entry tax) omitted, entry 54 substituted (State sales tax now only on petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas, ATF and alcoholic liquor for human consumption, excluding inter-State and international sales), entry 55 (advertisements) omitted, entry 62 substituted (entertainment taxes only to the extent levied by a Panchayat, Municipality, Regional or District Council).
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Parenthetical labels (entry tax, advertisements, newspapers) are our glosses from the Constitution; the Act text only substitutes or omits the entry numbers.

claim: Section 18 of the Act: Parliament shall by law, on the Council's recommendation, provide compensation to the States for loss of revenue arising from GST implementation 'for a period of five years'. Section 19: inconsistent State tax laws continue until amended or for one year from commencement, whichever is earlier.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council

claim: Section 15 of the Act adds Article 279A to the list in the proviso to Article 368(2)(a), i.e. a later change to Article 279A needs ratification by the State legislatures as for other federal provisions.
source: The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part II s.1, No.55, 8 Sept 2016 (Legislative Dept, e-Gazette)
second_source: Same Act, copy hosted by the GST Council
note: Reading of the proviso itself (half of the States' ratification) is from the Constitution, not read here; the Act text only adds 279A to clause (a) of the proviso.

claim: The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the 2014 Amendment Bill (as recited by the Supreme Court) says GST shall replace a number of indirect taxes levied by the Union and the States and is intended to 'remove cascading effect of taxes' and 'provide for a common national market for goods and services'.
as_of: 2014 (Bill); exact date not in saved sources
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
note: The quoted words match the question's phrase. The Bill itself (Bill 192 of 2014) was not read at Lok Sabha/Sansad; the Court's recital is the source. Marked CONFIRMED for the wording only. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] The date 24 Dec 2014 is not in any saved source (Court gives only the year; GST Council page says 2014). Quote matches Court para 23, pp.57-58.

claim: Passage and commencement: the Bill passed Rajya Sabha on 3 August 2016 and Lok Sabha on 8 August 2016, was passed by more than 15 States and got the President's assent on 8 September 2016; the notification bringing Art 279A into force from 12 September 2016 was issued on 10 September 2016; all sections were brought into effect by notifications of 16 September 2016; the Council's first meeting was on 22-23 September 2016.
source: GST Council, 'The GST Council' page
note: Year of introduction of the Bill (122nd Amendment Bill, Dec 2014) is only in the Court's judgment (claim -16), not on this page.

claim: GST was introduced on 1 July 2017. CBIC states the aim of 'amalgamating a large number of Central and State taxes into a single tax' was 'to mitigate cascading or double taxation in a major way and pave the way for a common national market'.
source: CBIC, 'GST - Concept & Status', updated 1 Jan 2018

claim: Central taxes subsumed (CBIC): Central Excise Duty; Duties of Excise (Medicinal and Toilet Preparations); Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance); Additional Duties of Excise (Textiles and Textile Products); Additional Duties of Customs (CVD); Special Additional Duty of Customs (SAD); Service Tax; and cesses and surcharges relating to supply of goods or services. State taxes subsumed: State VAT, Central Sales Tax, Purchase Tax, Luxury Tax, Entry Tax (all forms), Entertainment Tax (except by local bodies), taxes on advertisements, taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling, and State cesses and surcharges relating to supply of goods or services.
source: CBIC, 'GST - Concept & Status', updated 1 Jan 2018
note: Basic Customs Duty, alcohol and the five petroleum goods remain outside (see -07, -08).

claim: Court on the objective: reading the 2014 Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons, the debates and speeches shows Arts 246A and 279A aimed at cooperative federalism and harmony; the mischief to be remedied was the complexity and cascading effect of a multiplicity of taxes.
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
page_or_section: Part C, para 24 (judgment p.58) and para 51 (p.82)
note: Para ~p.82 is the passage beginning 'reading of the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the 2014 Amendment Bill'. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Page fixed: para 24 (mischief, cascading) is p.58 only; the cooperative federalism and harmony passage is para 51 on p.82.

claim: The Supreme Court held that GST Council recommendations are not binding on the Union and the States: deletion of Art 279B (the dispute authority of the 2011 Bill) and the structure of Arts 246A and 279A show Parliament meant them to have 'persuasive value'; the Government is bound only when exercising rule-making power under the CGST and IGST Acts.
source: Union of India v Mohit Minerals Pvt Ltd, Civil Appeal 1390 of 2022, Supreme Court, 19 May 2022 (Court's own copy)
note: The judgment's own text says 'Article 279(1)' in 148(i)(a) where it means 279A(1).

claim: Gross GST revenue FY 2025-26 (April-March) was Rs 22,27,096 crore, up 8.3% on Rs 20,55,515 crore in FY 2024-25 (both exclude compensation cess); net GST revenue Rs 19,34,766 crore; total refunds Rs 2,92,330 crore. Figures are provisional.
source: GSTN/GST Council: GST Gross and Net Collections as on 31/03/2026
page_or_section: Table, 'Total Gross GST Revenue' row; Yearly columns
second_source: PIB Backgrounder 'Nine Years of GST', 30 June 2026

claim: PIB: the number of GST taxpayers rose from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to 1.65 crore as of May 2026, which it reads as greater formalisation; gross GST collection was about Rs 7.4 lakh crore in 2017-18 and about Rs 22.27 lakh crore in 2025-26.
source: PIB Backgrounder 'Nine Years of GST', 30 June 2026
page_or_section: 'Nine Years of GST' backgrounder, opening section
note: 2017-18 is the nine months July 2017 to March 2018 (see 2019-GS3-1 ledger, Lok Sabha reply 2272).

claim: On 3 Sept 2025 the 56th Council recommended replacing the 4-tier rate structure with a 2-rate structure (standard 18%, merit 5%) plus a 40% rate for a few goods and services, and listed 'correction of long-pending inverted duty structure' for man-made textiles and in fertilizers.
value: rate slabs cut; inverted duty fixed
source: PIB / GST Council: Recommendations of the 56th GST Council meeting, 3 Sept 2025
page_or_section: PDF p.1 (4-tier to 2 rates, 40%); PDF p.3 (inverted duty bullets)
note: Official admission that rate multiplicity and inverted duty (a form of tax stuck in the chain) persisted for eight years. It is the Council's own statement, not an independent audit. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Page fixed: inverted-duty bullets are on p.3, not pp.1-2. Fertilizer bullet does not say long-pending; only the textile bullet does.

claim: Under the 56th Council's recommendation, rate changes took effect 22 Sept 2025 for services and most goods, but pan masala, gutkha, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, unmanufactured tobacco and bidi stayed at existing GST and compensation cess 'till loan and interest payment obligations under the compensation cess account are completely discharged'.
source: PIB / GST Council: Recommendations of the 56th GST Council meeting, 3 Sept 2025
second_source: GST Council Newsletter Dec 2025: cess on specified pan masala and tobacco withdrawn from 1 Feb 2026 (Notification 03/2025-Compensation Cess (Rate), 31.12.2025)
note: Notification text itself not read; the Council's newsletter reports it. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Page fixed (p.4 only). The press release records a recommendation; that rate changes took effect 22 Sept 2025 rests on notifications not read here.
